title: Application security hardening and threat modelling
subtitle: I review my own public endpoints, fix findings in severity order with explicit probes, and re-run the threat model when a fix breaks the world.

stats.label: lines of Python in the security-module library

lede: The OAuth registration lock I reverted within a day is the worked example. I treat security as a threat-model question: I close holes quickly, and I reverse my own fix when the facts show it sits at the wrong layer. Auth and access plane has an OAuth authorization server that is public on purpose: commercial AI assistants self-register as clients and connect to my private tool estate through it. Its traffic analytics showed me exposure, so I ran a hardening pass. I triaged the findings by severity, applied the smallest fix for each, and paired each fix with a probe, so every fix has a test that shows it doing its job.
quote: A security change that locks out every legitimate client is a failed change, and I reverse it on the facts even when it looked like hardening.
evidence: Application security hardening: a public OAuth authorization server's findings triaged by severity, each fixed with the smallest change and paired with one of 7 acceptance probes.
Threat modelling: a fail-closed registration gate reversed when it locked out every assistant, the control kept at the consent screen and pending-client lifetime raised from 1 hour to 30 days.
Defence in depth for web services: NGINX with TLS 1.2 and 1.3, HSTS and per-endpoint rate limits, a sandboxed systemd unit, and a 9,000-line Python security library kept off the request path.
author: Corey James
